title: the word Pope Francis kept saying
hook: the word Pope Francis kept saying

segments.voice: Yesterday: Francis of Assisi, the rich kid who gave it all back. Your line was lord, make me an instrument. Today, the pope who took his name. Day eighteen.

In 2013, a man from Buenos Aires who used to ride the bus to work became pope and took a name no pope had ever used: Francis, after the saint from Assisi you met yesterday. One word kept coming up, in sermons, in interviews, off the cuff to crowds. He called a whole year after it. He titled a book after it. Asked once, early on, to describe himself, he said, in effect: a sinner the Lord has looked upon. Pope Francis led the Church until his death in 2025. Today, his word: mercy.
screen: `A POPE WHO RODE THE BUS.` → `ONE WORD KEPT COMING UP.` → `A SINNER THE LORD LOOKED UPON.`

segments.voice: The Latin word is misericordia. Inside it are two smaller words: miser, wretched, in trouble, and cor, the heart. Mercy is a heart that goes out to someone in misery. Not a verdict. A heart. The Bible's Hebrew has a word for it that comes from the word for a mother's womb, the kind of love you feel for a child you carried. Luke's Gospel puts it at the center of what Jesus asks, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." Pope Francis took his motto from an old sermon by Bede, an English monk, about the day Jesus called Matthew, a tax collector everyone despised. Jesus looked at him, Bede says, with mercy, and chose him. In Latin: miserando atque eligendo. By having mercy, and by choosing. Francis said that was his own story. That's where today's line comes from. Francis kept saying that people who can't show mercy have often never let themselves receive it. You can't give away what you've never been handed. So the first step is to accept it: to let God, or someone, look at you with mercy and choose you anyway, the way Jesus looked at Matthew. For some people, the hardest one to show mercy to is themselves. Then it flows outward: forgiving, feeding, visiting, going toward people in trouble. Catholics call these the works of mercy. Francis of Assisi kissing the leper's hand was the same heart. And confession, from day three, is the Church saying it out loud: you're forgiven.
screen: `MISERICORDIA — A HEART FOR THE WRETCHED.` · `BE YE THEREFORE MERCIFUL.` · `BY HAVING MERCY, AND BY CHOOSING.` · `YOU CAN'T GIVE WHAT YOU WERE NEVER HANDED.` · then, large: `START WITH YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Bring to mind one thing you haven't quite forgiven yourself for, if there is one. Something small is fine. Picture someone who loves you looking at it, and at you, without flinching. Not excusing it. Just looking at you with a heart that goes out to you. Breathe slowly, and let yourself be looked at like that. If you pray, you can let that look be God's.
Mercy. Misericordia: a heart that goes out to someone in trouble, received first, then given away. Eighteenth word.
Your line: start with yourself. Mercy received is the only kind you can pass on. Day eighteen.

howItsDone: Catholics practice the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, visiting the sick and forgiving injuries, and celebrate Divine Mercy Sunday on the Sunday after Easter.

notes: Title updated 2026-10-06 from 'the word Francis (the pope) can't stop saying' to 'the word Pope Francis kept saying': Pope Francis died on April 21, 2025, and the script already says he 'led the Church until his death in 2025'. Confirm the date.

Pope Francis quotations are paraphrased (all modern and under copyright): 'a sinner whom the Lord has looked upon' (2013 interview), the book The Name of God Is Mercy (2016), the Jubilee Year of Mercy (2015–16). Confirm.
'People who can't show mercy have often never received it' paraphrases a recurring theme in his preaching, not a single quotation. Confirm.
Bede's homily (Homily 1.21) and the motto miserando atque eligendo; confirm reference.
Hebrew rachamim from rechem (womb): standard; confirm.
Riding the bus in Buenos Aires: widely reported; confirm.
